To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the prevalence of cancer in the French elderly is higher than that found in other studies, and that the discrepancy between self-report and cancer registry is higher in the elderly than in the younger population.
the prevalence of cancer among the elderly in the south-western France was underestimated by self-reports and that the underestimation was more pronounced among men than among women.
the prevalence of cancer in the general elderly population is lower than previously reported.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the prevalence of cancer in the population of the elderly.
the study of the relationship between cancer and ageing and the impact of cancer on the elderly.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the self-reported cancer is not reliable, and the use of this information in epidemiological studies should be avoided.
the self-report method is not suitable to be used for the assessment of the prevalence of cancer in the general population.
self-reported cancer data should be used with caution and should be interpreted in conjunction with registry data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prevalence of self-reported cancer is underestimated and is related to the site of the tumor, to the time of occurrence and to the age at which the cancer occurred.
cancer is not a frequent cause of death in elderly people and that it is a very rare cause of disability in the elderly.
the prevalence of cancer in elderly persons is underestimated when relying on self-reports.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prevalence of cancer is underestimated in elderly persons.
the prevalence of self-reported cancer among the elderly is much higher than the actual number of cancer cases in the population.
self-reported data on cancer is unreliable and should not be used to study cancer in the elderly.
